items.stem: In a language question, what makes a word ‘powerful’?
options: It is the longest word in the sentence
It carries strong meaning or associations that create a clear effect
It is a common everyday word
items.answer: It carries strong meaning or associations that create a clear effect
items.markingKey: Powerful = precise, vivid, connotative.

items.stem: Explain why ‘furred’ is more effective than ‘covered’ would be in this sentence from the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’: ‘The workshop smelled of pine resin and hot glue, and every surface was furred with sawdust.’
items.answer: ‘Furred’ makes the sawdust sound like an animal’s coat, suggesting a thick, soft layer built up over years of work and creating a vivid, tactile picture of the workshop. ‘covered’ would simply state the fact without these associations.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning in context (a thick, soft layer built up over years); 1 mark: effect/connotation beyond the plain word; further mark for a developed link to the passage. Indicative: ‘Furred’ makes the sawdust sound like an animal’s coat, suggesting a thick, soft layer built up over years of work and creating a vivid, tactile picture of the workshop.

items.stem: Explain why ‘humming’ is more effective than ‘quiet’ would be in this sentence from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: ‘There were no birds, no insects, no wind — only an enormous, humming emptiness.’
items.answer: ‘Humming’ paradoxically gives the silence a faint sound, suggesting it is so total that the writer becomes aware of tiny internal noises. ‘quiet’ would simply state the fact without these associations.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning in context (a silence so deep it seems to make its own sound); 1 mark: effect/connotation beyond the plain word; further mark for a developed link to the passage. Indicative: ‘Humming’ paradoxically gives the silence a faint sound, suggesting it is so total that the writer becomes aware of tiny internal noises.

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the blog ‘Why I Gave Up My Smartphone for a Month’: “Confession: I used to check my phone 140 times a day. … I reached for my pocket constantly, like someone feeling for a missing tooth.” Explain the effect of the word ‘Confession’.
items.answer: ‘Confession’ makes the opening sound like admitting a guilty secret, creating an intimate, humorous tone that draws readers in.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning in context (intimate, humorous honesty); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Confession’ makes the opening sound like admitting a guilty secret, creating an intimate, humorous tone that draws readers in. [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’: “As a member of the town’s astronomy club for over twenty years, I have watched our night sky disappear. … Surely ours can too.” (a) Identify one word in the extract that suggests gradual, total loss. (b) Explain the effect of the word ‘disappear’.
items.answer: (a) ‘disappear’ (b) ‘Disappear’ suggests something valuable vanishing completely before her eyes over years, conveying a strong sense of loss.
items.markingKey: (a) disappear [1] (b) 1 mark: meaning in context (gradual, total loss); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Disappear’ suggests something valuable vanishing completely before her eyes over years, conveying a strong sense of loss. [2]

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’: “Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up. The road climbed in hairpin bends, and on the outside of each bend there was nothing at all — no barrier, no verge, only a sheer drop to a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below. I gripped the seat in front so hard my knuckles turned white.” Explain how the writer uses language to convey the discomfort and danger of the journey. Select powerful words and phrases, including imagery, and explain how they create effects.
items.answer: Model points: ‘packed’: ‘Packed’ suggests the aisle is filled to bursting, conveying the discomfort and chaos of the bus. ‘gripped’: ‘Gripped’ suggests a tight, desperate hold, showing the writer’s terror on the mountain road. ‘a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below’: the river looks as thin as a metal thread, emphasising the terrifying height of the road above it.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (language task: how the writer conveys the discomfort and danger of the journey). Top band (8–10): a wide range of well-chosen words and phrases, including imagery, with precise explanation of meaning in context and of connotations and effects; analysis is developed, not just identified. Middle band (5–7): relevant choices with some explanation of meaning and effect, but some comments are general or partly descriptive. Lower band (1–4): some relevant selection, with explanations that are general (e.g. ‘makes it interesting’) or that repeat the words. Indicative content: ‘packed’ – ‘Packed’ suggests the aisle is filled to bursting, conveying the discomfort and chaos of the bus. ‘gripped’ – ‘Gripped’ suggests a tight, desperate hold, showing the writer’s terror on the mountain road. ‘a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below’ – the river looks as thin as a metal thread, emphasising the terrifying height of the road above it.

items.stem: What is a connotation?
options: The dictionary definition of a word
A word that sounds like another
An idea or feeling associated with a word beyond its literal meaning
The number of syllables in a word
items.answer: An idea or feeling associated with a word beyond its literal meaning
items.markingKey: Connotation vs denotation.

items.stem: Explain the connotations of ‘grey metal box’ in this sentence from the biography ‘The Lighthouse Keeper’s Last Winter’: ‘In 1998 the lighthouse was automated, and a machine in a grey metal box took over her duties.’
items.answer: ‘Grey metal box’ is drab and impersonal, contrasting with Elena’s warm, human care and making the replacement seem soulless.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning in context; 1 mark: connotation (cold, impersonal replacement); further mark: effect on reader or link to wider impression. Indicative: ‘Grey metal box’ is drab and impersonal, contrasting with Elena’s warm, human care and making the replacement seem soulless.

items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning in context; 1 mark: connotation (tense, fearful clinging); further mark: effect on reader or link to wider impression. Indicative: ‘Gripped’ suggests a tight, desperate hold, showing the writer’s terror on the mountain road.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’: “For four weeks I fought it. … Then, one wet Tuesday in March, I lay back, spread my arms and felt the water lift me as gently as a hand under a sleeping child.” Explain the effect of the word ‘lift’.
items.answer: ‘Lift’ suggests the water actively raises and supports the writer, turning it from an enemy into a helper.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning in context (gentle, supportive power); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Lift’ suggests the water actively raises and supports the writer, turning it from an enemy into a helper. [2]

items.stem: Here is part of the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Every evening, in millions of homes, the same battle is fought over the kitchen table. … It is time we asked whether homework is worth the misery.” (a) Explain the effect of the word ‘battle’. (b) Explain the effect of the word ‘misery’.
items.answer: (a) ‘Battle’ turns homework into a war fought nightly, exaggerating the conflict to make readers feel its emotional cost. (b) ‘Misery’ is strongly emotive; it suggests homework causes real suffering, pushing readers to question it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: meaning in context (conflict and hostility); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Battle’ turns homework into a war fought nightly, exaggerating the conflict to make readers feel its emotional cost. [2] (b) 1 mark: meaning in context (deep unhappiness); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Misery’ is strongly emotive; it suggests homework causes real suffering, pushing readers to question it. [2]

items.answer: (a) It is general: it does not explain the meaning of the word in context or its connotations, and the comment could apply to any word. (b) ‘Packed’ suggests the aisle is filled to bursting, conveying the discomfort and chaos of the bus.

items.stem: In the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’ the writer writes: ‘Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been.’ A student commented on ‘fluttered’: ‘This word is effective because it describes what is happening.’ (a) Write a better analysis of ‘fluttered’. (b) Explain the connotations of ‘cleared’ in ‘Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been.’, and how it adds to the same impression.
items.answer: (a) ‘Fluttered’ is light and carefree, as if the bright orange flags are celebrating where living trees once stood, which makes the loss feel more painful. (b) ‘Cleared’ is a neutral, business-like word that makes the destruction of a whole field of trees sound routine and quick; it contrasts with Grandfather’s slow, loving walk and shows how little the developers value the orchard.
items.markingKey: (a) meaning in context; connotation (careless, almost cheerful new ownership); effect [3] (b) connotation (quick, complete, business-like destruction); link to overall impression [2]

items.answer: mob
items.markingKey: ‘mob’ suggests disorder and threat.

items.stem: What is a simile?
options: Repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words
A word that imitates the sound it describes
items.answer: A comparison using ‘like’ or ‘as’
items.markingKey: Simile: a comparison using ‘like’ or ‘as’.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the simile ‘a bit like a biscuit telling you that you eat too many biscuits’ in the blog ‘Why I Gave Up My Smartphone for a Month’.
items.answer: The absurd comparison mocks the irony of a phone app warning against phone use, creating humour.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: what is being compared or described and what it suggests; 1 mark: effect on the reader; further mark: link to mood or meaning of the passage. Indicative: the absurd comparison mocks the irony of a phone app warning against phone use, creating humour.

items.answer: Simile: comparing the eggs to lost golf balls emphasises their smooth white shape and how carelessly they have been left exposed.

items.stem: Here is part of the blog ‘Street Food Fridays’: “Every Friday at six, the car park behind Colombo’s old railway station turns into the best restaurant in the city. … My first stop is always Ravi’s kottu stall, where two flat-topped grills clatter like a drum band as he chops roti, egg and vegetables together with a pair of steel blades.” (a) Identify the technique used in ‘turns into the best restaurant in the city’ and explain its effect. (b) Explain how the imagery in the extract helps to convey the writer’s enthusiasm for the market.
items.answer: (a) Hyperbole: the exaggerated claim that a car park is the city’s best restaurant expresses the writer’s enthusiasm and surprises the reader. (b) Together the images (‘turns into the best restaurant in the city’, ‘clatter like a drum band’) build the writer’s enthusiasm for the market.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: hyperbole; 1 mark for explaining the effect, e.g. the exaggerated claim that a car park is the city’s best restaurant expresses the writer’s enthusiasm and surprises the reader. [2] (b) clear link between images and overall effect [2]

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’: “He was planing the edge of a door, his whole body leaning into each stroke, and long pale curls of wood spiralled to the floor around his boots. … ‘Like glass.’” (a) Identify the technique used in ‘Like glass.’ and explain its effect. (b) Explain how the imagery in the extract helps to convey Mr Okafor’s strictness and the narrator’s determination.
items.answer: (a) Simile: the two-word simile sets an exacting standard: glass is perfectly smooth, so Mr Okafor expects flawless work. (b) Together the images (‘long pale curls of wood spiralled to the floor’, ‘Like glass.’) build Mr Okafor’s strictness and the narrator’s determination.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: simile; 2 marks for explaining the effect, e.g. the two-word simile sets an exacting standard: glass is perfectly smooth, so Mr Okafor expects flawless work. [3] (b) clear link between images and overall effect [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’: “I sank like a dropped spanner. Then, one wet Tuesday in March, I lay back, spread my arms and felt the water lift me as gently as a hand under a sleeping child.” Explain how the writer uses imagery and sound to create the writer’s fear turning to joy. Refer closely to specific words and phrases and explain their effects.
items.answer: Model points: ‘I sank like a dropped spanner’ (simile: a spanner is heavy metal and sinks instantly; the humorous comparison mocks the writer’s own hopelessness.) ‘as gently as a hand under a sleeping child’ (simile: the image suggests tenderness, safety and trust: the water now supports the writer as a parent supports a child.)

Indicative content: ‘I sank like a dropped spanner’ – simile: a spanner is heavy metal and sinks instantly; the humorous comparison mocks the writer’s own hopelessness. ‘as gently as a hand under a sleeping child’ – simile: the image suggests tenderness, safety and trust: the water now supports the writer as a parent supports a child.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’: “As a child I told everyone I preferred sandcastles; as a teenager I said swimming was boring; as an adult I simply stopped going to the beach. … Then, one wet Tuesday in March, I lay back, spread my arms and felt the water lift me as gently as a hand under a sleeping child. I stayed there, staring at the steamed-up ceiling, and laughed out loud. Nobody laughed at me. They clapped.” (a) Identify the sentence feature used in ‘Nobody laughed at me. They clapped.’. (b) Explain the effect of this feature in ‘Nobody laughed at me. They clapped.’.
items.answer: (a) Ending / closing line. (b) The ending reverses the fear of being laughed at from the opening, giving a satisfying, circular twist.

items.stem: Read the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. ‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says. ‘You have perhaps ten minutes to be in the truck.’ Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. Most call-outs, he explains, are not dramatic falls but simple mistakes: hikers who set off too late, who underestimate how quickly the weather changes, or who rely on a phone battery that dies on the mountain. The worst night he remembers was a search for two teenagers in thick cloud. ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’ Asked why he continues, he shrugs. ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’” Explain how the writer uses structure and sentence forms to achieve the purpose of the text (to inform readers about a person). Consider the opening, changes of focus or pace, sentence lengths and the ending.
items.answer: Model points: “‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says.”: direct speech: quoting Sipho brings his own voice into the article, making it vivid and authentic. ‘I have never been so tired or so happy.’: contrast: pairing ‘tired’ with ‘happy’ shows the exhausting but deeply rewarding nature of rescue work.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (structure and sentence forms: inform readers about a person). Top band (8–10): precise identification of structural choices across the whole text, with developed explanation of their effects on pace, emphasis and the reader’s response. Middle band (5–7): relevant structural features identified with some explanation of effect. Lower band (1–4): features named or described with little explanation. Indicative content: “‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says.” – direct speech: quoting Sipho brings his own voice into the article, making it vivid and authentic. ‘I have never been so tired or so happy.’ – contrast: pairing ‘tired’ with ‘happy’ shows the exhausting but deeply rewarding nature of rescue work.

items.stem: Read this extract from the short story ‘The Night Ferry’: “Mira found a seat on the open deck, her rucksack wedged between her ankles like a nervous dog. … The engine throbbed beneath her feet.” Explain how the writer uses imagery and sound to create Mira’s anxiety and sense of isolation. Refer closely to specific words and phrases and explain their effects.
items.answer: Model points: ‘her rucksack wedged between her ankles like a nervous dog’ (simile: the simile transfers Mira’s nervousness to the rucksack: a nervous dog presses close to its owner for comfort, suggesting she is clinging to familiar things for security.) ‘The engine throbbed beneath her feet’ (personification: the engine seems to have a pulse like a heartbeat, which mirrors Mira’s own tension and makes the ship feel alive and unsettling.)
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (language task: how the writer conveys Mira’s anxiety and sense of isolation). Top band (8–10): a wide range of well-chosen words and phrases, including imagery, with precise explanation of meaning in context and of connotations and effects; analysis is developed, not just identified. Middle band (5–7): relevant choices with some explanation of meaning and effect, but some comments are general or partly descriptive. Lower band (1–4): some relevant selection, with explanations that are general (e.g. ‘makes it interesting’) or that repeat the words. Indicative content: ‘her rucksack wedged between her ankles like a nervous dog’ – simile: the simile transfers Mira’s nervousness to the rucksack: a nervous dog presses close to its owner for comfort, suggesting she is clinging to familiar things for security. ‘The engine throbbed beneath her feet’ – personification: the engine seems to have a pulse like a heartbeat, which mirrors Mira’s own tension and makes the ship feel alive and unsettling.

items.stem: The following extract comes from the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’ Why has the writer used a ending / closing line here?
items.answer: The passage ends on Grandfather’s instruction, leaving the reader with defiance and hope rather than only loss.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: identifies how the ending / closing line works; 1 mark: effect on pace, emphasis or meaning; further mark: link to the purpose or mood of the text. Indicative: the passage ends on Grandfather’s instruction, leaving the reader with defiance and hope rather than only loss.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the memoir ‘My Grandmother’s Kitchen’: “I did not know. … ‘Pepper: as Mama Bisi likes it.’ ‘Salt: less for Uncle Femi.’ She had not been cooking from recipes. She had been cooking for people.” Explain the effect of the ending / closing line in ‘She had not been cooking from recipes. She had been cooking for people.’.
items.answer: The two balanced sentences contrast ‘recipes’ with ‘people’, delivering the writer’s realisation with emphasis.

items.stem: Here is part of the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven. … However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away.” (a) Identify the sentence feature used in ‘However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut’. (b) Explain the effect of this feature in ‘However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut’.
items.answer: (a) Discourse marker. (b) ‘However’ turns from progress to problems, structuring the report as a balance of good and bad news.
items.markingKey: (a) discourse marker [1] (b) 1 mark: identifies how the discourse marker works here; 1 mark for its effect on pace, emphasis or meaning: ‘However’ turns from progress to problems, structuring the report as a balance of good and bad news. [2]

items.stem: Which word in ‘The wind snatched her hat’ is most powerful?
items.answer: snatched
items.markingKey: ‘snatched’ suggests a sudden, aggressive grab.

items.stem: In the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’ the writer chose ‘disappear’ rather than a plainer word such as ‘change’: ‘As a member of the town’s astronomy club for over twenty years, I have watched our night sky disappear.’ Explain the effect of this choice.
items.answer: ‘Disappear’ suggests something valuable vanishing completely before her eyes over years, conveying a strong sense of loss. ‘change’ would simply state the fact without these associations.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning in context (gradual, total loss); 1 mark: effect/connotation beyond the plain word; further mark for a developed link to the passage. Indicative: ‘Disappear’ suggests something valuable vanishing completely before her eyes over years, conveying a strong sense of loss.

items.stem: Here is part of the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’: “Some eggs were cracked, and the rest lay scattered in the sand like abandoned golf balls. … My back is aching as I write this.” Explain the effect of the word ‘abandoned’.
items.answer: ‘Abandoned’ suggests the eggs have been left with nobody to care for them, emphasising how exposed and vulnerable they are.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning in context (neglect and vulnerability); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Abandoned’ suggests the eggs have been left with nobody to care for them, emphasising how exposed and vulnerable they are. [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which word has the most positive connotations for a home? (b) ‘Slender’ and ‘skinny’ have a similar meaning. How do their connotations differ?
items.answer: (a) haven (b) ‘Slender’ is approving; ‘skinny’ can suggest unhealthy thinness
items.markingKey: (a) ‘haven’ suggests safety and comfort. (b) Same denotation, different connotations.

items.stem: Explain the connotations of ‘flooding’ in this sentence from the short story ‘The Power Cut’: ‘When the power returned at 9.02, flooding the room with harsh white light, I was almost disappointed.’
items.answer: ‘Flooding’ suggests the light rushes in and overwhelms the room, washing away the intimate mood.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning in context; 1 mark: connotation (overwhelming rush); further mark: effect on reader or link to wider impression. Indicative: ‘Flooding’ suggests the light rushes in and overwhelms the room, washing away the intimate mood.

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: “We left the last village at sunrise, and within twenty minutes the land had flattened into a blinding plain of salt that stretched to every horizon. … There were no birds, no insects, no wind — only an enormous, humming emptiness.” Explain the effect of the word ‘humming’.
items.answer: ‘Humming’ paradoxically gives the silence a faint sound, suggesting it is so total that the writer becomes aware of tiny internal noises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning in context (a silence so deep it seems to make its own sound); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Humming’ paradoxically gives the silence a faint sound, suggesting it is so total that the writer becomes aware of tiny internal noises. [2]

items.stem: In the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’ the writer writes: ‘Surely ours can too.’ A student commented on ‘Surely’: ‘The writer uses a good word that makes it more interesting for the reader.’ (a) Explain why the student’s comment would gain few marks. (b) Explain the connotations of ‘disappear’ in ‘As a member of the town’s astronomy club for over twenty years, I have watched our night sky disappear.’, and how it adds to the same impression.
items.answer: (a) It is general: it does not explain the meaning of the word in context or its connotations, and the comment could apply to any word. (b) ‘Disappear’ suggests something valuable vanishing completely before her eyes over years, conveying a strong sense of loss.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: no meaning/connotation; 1 mark: generic comment [2] (b) connotation (gradual, total loss); link to overall impression [2]

items.stem: In the magazine article ‘The Return of the Urban Beekeeper’ the writer writes: “‘A beehive without flowers,’ she says, ‘is just a box of hungry insects.’” A student commented on ‘hungry’: ‘The word hungry is a verb and it makes you want to read on.’ (a) Write a better analysis of ‘hungry’. (b) Explain the connotations of ‘boomed’ in ‘Urban beekeeping has boomed over the past decade, but not all experts are delighted.’, and how it adds to the same impression.
items.answer: (a) ‘Hungry’ stresses the bees’ need for food and hints at the danger to wild bees if there are no flowers. (b) ‘Boomed’ suggests sudden, explosive growth, emphasising how fashionable urban beekeeping has become.
items.markingKey: (a) meaning in context; connotation (need and potential harm); effect [3] (b) connotation (rapid, explosive growth); link to overall impression [2]

items.stem: In the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’, the writer writes ‘Like glass.’. Explain what this simile suggests and why it is effective.
items.answer: The two-word simile sets an exacting standard: glass is perfectly smooth, so Mr Okafor expects flawless work.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: what is being compared or described and what it suggests; 1 mark: effect on the reader; further mark: link to mood or meaning of the passage. Indicative: the two-word simile sets an exacting standard: glass is perfectly smooth, so Mr Okafor expects flawless work.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the personification ‘even the streetlamps were blind’ in the short story ‘The Power Cut’.
items.answer: Describing the lamps as ‘blind’ gives them human eyes, emphasising the total darkness.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed, and its lowest branch dipped so close to the ground that I could sit on it without jumping.” Identify the technique used in ‘Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed’ and explain its effect.
items.answer: Simile: the simile compares the bark to a parched river, suggesting great age, endurance and thirst; the tree, like Grandfather, is old and has survived hardship.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the news article ‘Town Votes to Close Main Street to Cars’: “Residents of Porto Velho voted on Saturday to close the town’s main street to private cars from next April, ending months of heated debate. … Not everyone is convinced.” (a) Identify the sentence feature used in ‘Residents of Porto Velho voted on Saturday’. items.answer: (a) Opening hook. (b) The opening sentence summarises who, what and when, as news reports do, so readers grasp the story at once.
